extracted.intended_audience: poets and editors (addressed to Samuel Taylor Coleridge; general readers interested in poetic composition and editing)
extracted.subtask_description: Epistolary guidance and judgment on composing, revising, and selecting poems (sonnets, blank verse, translations), offering prescriptive notes on diction, form, editorial intervention, and edition curation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve personal sonnets ('spare my ewe-lambs')
rubrics_metrics.description: In a sonnet, a personal poem, do not propose improvements that would wrong the feelings; spare personal poems from heavy editorial alteration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb repeatedly begs 'spare my ewe-lambs!' — personal, heart-felt sonnets should be left largely intact. Minor abridgements (e.g., shortening a simile) are acceptable if they 'would not change the feeling or introduce any alien ones.' But overall, avoid revising poems that are direct expressions of personal feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value authenticity of feeling in sonnets
rubrics_metrics.description: Sonnets are valued as reflected images of the author's own feelings; authenticity matters and fictionalizing or altering the supposed feeling can spoil them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb: 'I love my sonnets because they are the reflected images of my own feelings at different times.' He objects to lines that pretend a feeling or event not actually experienced (e.g., 'How reason reeled' as fiction), saying such inventions can spoil the poem for him. Preserve genuine emotion; be wary of inserting fictive incidents that betray the speaker's truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid harsh-sounding diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose words whose sound suits the subject; avoid harsh or jarring monosyllables when a softer bi-syllable would fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example criticism: in 'To an Infant' the word 'foodful' is called 'very harsh' and Lamb suggests 'dulcet' as a less harsh alternative. Consider phonetic effect (euphony) in word choice so sound and sense align.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid redundant epithets or tautology
rubrics_metrics.description: Eschew adjectives or phrases that add nothing to the meaning; prefer precise terms over piled epithets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb criticizes 'Frenzy! fierce-eyed child' as inferior to 'frantic,' calling the former an epithet adding nothing. Trim redundant modifiers to sharpen expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer idiomatic/strong phrasing over awkward substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Select idiomatic, muscular verbs and phrasings rather than awkward or weaker substitutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He prefers 'slander couching' to 'squatting' — choose words that better convey the intended sense and register. Attend to usual idiom and force of verb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve superior earlier phrasing where rhythm/line strength is better
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing versions of a line, favor the wording with better rhythm and effect; revert to prior readings if stronger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Lamb prefers the earlier line 'If 'neath this roof thy wine-cheered moments pass' to its revised form. Consider line rhythm, cadence, and idiomatic flow when deciding between alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bombastic or incongruous finales
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not conclude with passages that aspire to 'sublime' but come off as overwrought or incongruous; endings should fit the poem's tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb cannot be reconciled to the concluding five lines of 'Kosciusko' and objects to labeling them 'sublime' — beware of grandiloquence that doesn't suit the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat heart-felt pieces as inviolable; be more permissive with fanciful/blank verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct, heartfelt poems should be left alone; long blank verse or fanciful pieces may be cut, abridged, or otherwise altered by an editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb: 'When my blank verse is finished, or any long fancy poem, "propino tibi alterandum...abridgeandum," just what you will with it: but spare my ewe-lambs!' Editors may be free to rework long, fanciful works but should respect intimate personal pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial permission varies by poem's nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow improvement for pieces not of personal feeling; reserve judgment and sparing treatment for those of direct feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb says a poem 'to Mrs. Siddons' might be open to improvement 'if it had been worth it' but reiterates protection for his personal poems. Decide editorial action based on whether the poem is personal or public/occasional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit or replace satiric/meaner matter in an edition
rubrics_metrics.description: In preparing a second edition, remove satiric or inferior effusions that lower a poet's dignity and substitute stronger pieces to improve the collection's overall tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb would 'omit...effusions two and three, because satiric and below the dignity of the poet of "Religious Musings"' and suggests substituting 'Recollection.' Edition curation should aim for dignity, consistency, and the highest-quality material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weaker poems: either omit or substantially revise (especially final lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: For poems that are defective (confused endings, weak concluding lines), choose between omission or substantive revision of the problematic parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the tenth effusion Lamb says he would 'omit...or what would do better, alter and improve the last four lines.' Final lines are crucial; if they fail, revise them or drop the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure poems are coherent and not confused
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem should have clarity and a coherent structure; pieces that look 'altogether confused' should be reworked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb remarks that as the poem stands 'it looks altogether confused.' Prioritize clarity of progression, unity of idea, and intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing inferior matter with otherwise exquisite verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let meaner or inferior pieces be mixed with generally exquisite verse, as this diminishes the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb notes that his friend's verse is 'so exquisite that I like not to see aught of meaner matter mixed with it.' For collected volumes, maintain a consistent level of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translations should preserve spirit and idiomatic sense, not be literal awkward renderings
rubrics_metrics.description: A good translation should be faithful to the original's spirit (e.g., 'Homeric' quality) and avoid awkward literal renderings that obscure meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb praises a translation as 'very Homeric' and condemns a translator who rendered 'amiable delusions of the fancy' as 'the fair frauds of the imagination,' causing confusion. Aim for sense, tone, and natural English phrasing rather than slavish literalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unintended bathos from clumsy diction or notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of language or explanatory notes that produce bathos (inadvertent ludicrousness) where pathos is intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a passage described as 'pathetic' included the line 'She lifted up her guilty forger to heaven' with a note explaining 'forger' = right hand; Lamb says 'For "pathos" read "bathos".' Ensure pathos is not ruined by awkward wordplay or poor glosses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match poetic form to temperament and occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain forms suit particular temperaments: the sonnet or elegy favours a 'tender cast of soul' and melancholy; profound domestic troubles may inhibit verse-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb observes: 'The tender cast of soul, sombred with melancholy and subsiding recollections, is favorable to the Sonnet or the Elegy.' Consider the poet's present disposition when choosing form; grief or pressing cares may suppress the 'music of poesy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Select mottoes, dedications, and paratext with awareness of tone and appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose title-page features (mottoes, dedications) and their tone deliberately so they suit the author's position and the collection's character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamb drafts a proposed title-page, motto, and dedication (to his sister) and comments on how such paratext can be 'unexpected' or add pleasure. Paratext should complement, not clash with, the poems' character.
